Every night, Mara dreams of a city where the moon hangs low and a masked stranger hunts her through deserted streets. When she wakes, her knuckles are bruised—and the stranger’s face is always a little clearer.

After a subway accident awakens her ability to enter other people’s dreams, Mara discovers that a secret organization is using the city’s sleepers to test a machine that can turn nightmares into real-world weapons. The masked hunter is its first creation: a fighter who can slip from dreams into waking life.

Mara tracks the machine’s inventor through a series of shifting dreamscapes, learning to shape her own fears into superpowers. In the final confrontation, she faces the hunter in a fist fight that begins in a collapsing dream arena and spills onto the streets at dawn. To defeat him, Mara must stop trying to outrun her nightmares—and take control of them.

When Mara wakes, she finds she can summon anything she touches in the dream into the real world. At first, she uses her strange new power to help people. But the stranger returns in her dreams, revealing that a force called the Sleeper is pulling entire neighborhoods into the dream city—and plans to bring the waking world with them.

Mara’s power grows with every night, but so does the danger. With the Sleeper’s nightmares spilling into daylight, she joins forces with a retired underground fighter who teaches her to defend herself the old-fashioned way: with her fists. Soon, Mara is battling shadow creatures in the real world and facing the Sleeper in a brutal fistfight inside the dream city, where every punch can reshape reality.

To stop the Sleeper, Mara must risk losing the one thing her power depends on: the ability to dream.

<<The Last Dreamer>>

Every night, Mara dreams of a city that doesn’t exist. Every morning, its buildings begin appearing in her hometown—and so do the monsters hunting through them.

Mara discovers she can pull objects out of her dreams, but only while she’s fighting. With each punch, she can summon a shield, a staircase, or a door where none existed. When her little brother falls asleep and can’t wake up, she enters the dream city to find him. There, she must face its ruler in a bare-knuckle fight, knowing that anything she imagines could become real—and anything she fears might, too.

<<The Last Dream Standing>>

Every night, exhausted paramedic Mara Voss dreams of the same underground boxing ring. The spectators have no faces, her opponent wears her dead brother’s jacket, and every punch she takes leaves a bruise that follows her into the morning.

Then, during a disastrous rescue, Mara discovers she can stop time—but only while holding her breath.

Searching for answers, she finds other people whose dreams have granted them impossible abilities. All have fought in the ring. All are being hunted by a sleep researcher who has learned to extract superpowers from the unconscious mind. His experiments are tearing down the boundary between dreams and reality, allowing nightmares to wander into the waking city.

Mara’s brother, presumed dead after volunteering for the researcher’s first trial, is still alive inside the shared dream. He has been fighting every night to keep its gates closed. But he is losing, and the researcher needs Mara’s time-stopping power to freeze the gates open permanently.

To rescue her brother, Mara must enter the ring willingly. There, her power works differently: every second she steals from time erases one of her memories. As she trades brutal punches with creatures built from her deepest fears, she begins forgetting the very person she came to save.

In the final fight, Mara faces the researcher, who can anticipate anything she consciously imagines. Unable to outthink him, she lets her brother coach her through a simple boxing combination they practiced as children. For once, she stops planning and trusts him. The last punch shatters the ring—and wakes everyone trapped inside.

At dawn, her brother finds her outside the ruined laboratory. Mara no longer recognizes his face. But when he raises his hands in their old sparring stance, she instinctively raises hers, laughing before she knows why.

# Business Proposal: Bremen Sweatshirt Co.

## *Executive Summary*
Bremen Sweatshirt Co. will design, produce, and sell premium quality sweatshirts inspired by the culture, maritime history, and modern spirit of Bremen, Germany. Our goal is to become the leading local apparel brand within three years while expanding into national and online markets. We aim to combine comfort, sustainability, and regional pride into every product we sell.

## *Market Analysis*
Bremen is a vibrant port city with a strong sense of local identity and a growing population of students, young professionals, and tourists. The demand for locally branded, high-quality streetwear is increasing, especially among consumers who value sustainable and ethically produced clothing. Competitor analysis shows a gap in the market for premium, Bremen-themed apparel that goes beyond generic tourist merchandise. Our target customers include:
- Local residents seeking regional pride apparel
- University students (University of Bremen, Jacobs University)
- Tourists visiting Bremen’s historic sites (Bremen Town Musicians, Marktplatz)
- Online shoppers across Germany interested in city-branded fashion

## *Product Line and Design Strategy*
Our initial collection will feature:
- Classic crewneck and hoodie sweatshirts with minimalist Bremen-themed graphics (e.g., the Town Musicians statue, the Weser river, maritime motifs)
- Premium organic cotton materials sourced from European suppliers
- Limited-edition seasonal designs celebrating local festivals (Freimarkt, Bremen Christmas Market)
- Customization options for corporate or event orders

We will prioritize sustainable production practices, using GOTS-certified organic cotton and eco-friendly printing methods to appeal to environmentally conscious consumers.

## *Marketing and Sales Strategy*
Our marketing plan will focus on building strong local brand recognition before scaling nationally:
- **Social Media Campaigns:** Instagram and TikTok content showcasing Bremen culture and behind-the-scenes production
- **Local Partnerships:** Collaborations with Bremen tourism boards, cafes, and university stores
- **Pop-Up Shops:** Seasonal presence at the Bremen Christmas Market and Freimarkt festival
- **E-Commerce Platform:** A dedicated online store with nationwide shipping and localized SEO targeting "Bremen apparel" and "German city fashion"
- **Influencer Collaborations:** Partnering with local micro-influencers to boost authenticity and reach

## *Financial Plan and Funding Requirements*
We are seeking initial funding of €75,000 to cover:
- Product design and prototyping: €10,000
- Manufacturing setup and first production run (2,000 units): €35,000
- Marketing and branding: €15,000
- E-commerce platform development: €8,000
- Operational reserve: €7,000

Projected revenue for Year 1 is €120,000, with a break-even point expected by month 10. By Year 3, we anticipate expanding into wholesale distribution with regional boutiques across Germany, targeting €500,000 in annual revenue.

## *Conclusion*
Bremen Sweatshirt Co. represents an opportunity to merge local heritage with modern fashion trends, delivering high-quality, sustainable apparel that resonates with both residents and visitors. With strategic investment and a targeted growth plan, our brand is positioned to become a beloved staple of Bremen’s cultural and commercial identity.

*Executive summary*

This proposal outlines the launch of a Bremen-based sweatshirt company with a distinctive local identity, a small initial product range, and an online-first sales model. The brand—provisionally named **Weser Thread**—would offer comfortable, durable sweatshirts inspired by Bremen’s neighborhoods, maritime heritage, and everyday city life.

The business would begin with a limited collection and test demand through direct online sales and local pop-ups before committing to larger production runs. The name is a working title and should be checked for trademark and domain availability before use.

*Brand and product concept*

The company’s position would be **locally rooted, design-led, and built for regular wear**, rather than dependent on souvenir-style graphics or short-lived trends.

Initial range:
- Two sweatshirt styles: a classic crewneck and a relaxed-fit option.
- Three core colors, with a limited seasonal color or graphic.
- Designs influenced by Bremen’s architecture, riverfront, and independent creative culture.
- Clear information on fabric composition, fit, care, and manufacturing.

Prioritize quality, comfortable fabrics, and reliable construction. Where suppliers allow, use certified or recycled materials and publish specific, verifiable claims rather than broad statements such as “eco-friendly.”

The initial audience would include:
- Bremen residents and people with a connection to the city.
- Students and young professionals seeking distinctive casual clothing.
- Visitors looking for contemporary local designs.
- Customers elsewhere in Germany who respond to the Bremen-inspired brand story.

The company would compete with independent fashion labels and larger casualwear brands. Its differentiation would come from original local designs, a consistent visual identity, transparent product information, and a close relationship with Bremen customers.

*Sales and marketing strategy*

Launch with a direct-to-consumer online store to retain control over the customer experience and gather sales data. Support online sales with:
- Instagram and TikTok content showing designs, production, and local settings.
- Email sign-ups offering early access to the first collection.
- Collaborations with Bremen artists, photographers, or community groups.
- Weekend markets and pop-up events to let customers see and try the products.
- Selective wholesale outreach to local boutiques after direct sales are established.

A practical launch sequence is to share design previews, collect email sign-ups, offer a limited first drop, and review customer feedback before reordering. Avoid large paid-ad commitments until conversion rates and customer acquisition costs are understood.

*Operations and production*

Use a low-risk production approach at first: work with a print-on-demand provider or commission a small batch from a suitable European supplier. Compare suppliers on minimum order quantities, sample quality, lead times, fabric specifications, printing methods, shipping, and return arrangements.

Before placing a production order:
1. Order and inspect samples.
2. Test sizing and wash durability.
3. Confirm written specifications and delivery dates.
4. Calculate the full landed cost, including freight and packaging.
5. Set a clear process for handling defects and customer returns.

Initially, store inventory at home or with a small fulfillment provider if practical. Review sell-through by size, color, and design before expanding the range.

*Legal and administrative setup*

Before trading, the founder should confirm the appropriate business structure and registrations for Germany. This may include registering a trade (*Gewerbeanmeldung*) in Bremen, tax registration, and arranging bookkeeping and invoicing processes. The business should also check its responsibilities for:
- Textile-fibre composition and product labeling.
- Consumer information, pricing, returns, and online-store terms.
- Packaging registration and applicable packaging obligations in Germany.
- Data protection, cookie consent, and email marketing.
- Product safety and any applicable EU requirements.
- Trademark, business-name, and domain availability.

Requirements depend on the business model and products, so confirm them with the relevant authorities or qualified advisers before launch.

*Milestones and measures of success*

**Months 1–2:** Validate the brand concept, interview potential customers, select designs, obtain samples, and confirm legal and supplier requirements.

**Months 3–4:** Build the online store, create launch content, gather email sign-ups, and place a small first production order.

A Bremen sweatshirt company can be launched with a focused collection, controlled production risk, and strong local storytelling. The recommended approach is to validate demand through samples, pre-launch interest, and a small first run before investing in a broader range. A disciplined budget and clear supplier and compliance checks will give the business a stronger foundation for growth.

- **Early expansion:** Tang rulers reunited much of China after a period of division. Strong administration and relative **peace** helped farming, cities and trade prosper. But expansion also brought **war**: Tang armies fought to secure territory and influence in Central Asia and along the Silk Road.
- **Culture and commerce:** During more stable years, **peace** encouraged merchants, travelers and ideas to move across Asia. The capital, Chang’an, became a major cosmopolitan city. Buddhism spread widely, while Tang poetry and art flourished.
- **Rebellion and unrest:** In 755, the An Lushan Rebellion began. This devastating **war**—a major **civil war**—lasted until 763, caused enormous loss of life and weakened the dynasty. The **peace** that followed was fragile: regional military governors gained power, and further fighting broke out.
- **Decline:** Later rebellions, court struggles and conflicts with neighboring powers further eroded Tang authority. The dynasty could not restore lasting **peace**, and in 907 it fell, ushering in another era of division.

# The Tang Dynasty: A Balance of War and Peace

The Tang dynasty (618-907 CE) was a period marked by cycles of war followed by long stretches of peace, creating one of China's most celebrated golden ages. Understanding this era requires examining both the war campaigns that established Tang power and the peace that allowed civilization to flourish.

## The War for Establishment

The Tang dynasty emerged from war. Li Yuan and his son Li Shimin waged war against the crumbling Sui dynasty, using military conflict to seize control. This early war was necessary before peace could be established. Once the war ended in Tang victory, Emperor Taizong worked to transform war-torn China into a realm of peace.

## Expansion Through War, Maintained by Peace

Tang China engaged in war on multiple frontiers to expand its borders. Military campaigns—essentially wars of expansion—pushed Tang influence into Central Asia, Korea, and parts of Tibet. However, after each war concluded, administrators prioritized peace to consolidate gains. The Tang rulers understood that war alone could not sustain an empire; peace was essential for prosperity.

Trade along the Silk Road flourished specifically because of peace. Merchants could not operate during active war, so maintaining peace along these routes became a priority. This peace brought immense wealth, as goods flowed between China and distant lands.

## Cultural Peace and Achievement

The periods of peace under rulers like Emperor Taizong and Empress Wu Zetian allowed:

- Poetry and literature to flourish (Li Bai and Du Fu wrote during relative peace)
- Buddhism to spread without disruption
- Bureaucratic reforms to take root
- International diplomacy to replace war

Foreign dignitaries visited the peaceful Tang court, and the capital Chang'an became a symbol of peace and cosmopolitan exchange.

## The An Lushan Rebellion: Peace Shattered

This golden age of peace was shattered by the An Lushan Rebellion (755-763), a devastating civil war. This war killed millions and ended the great peace that had defined earlier Tang rule. After this war, the dynasty never fully recovered its former glory, though smaller periods of peace did return.

## Conclusion

The Tang dynasty demonstrates how war and peace intertwine in history—war built the empire, peace allowed it to flourish culturally and economically, and eventually renewed war led to its decline. The delicate balance between war and peace defined nearly three centuries of Chinese civilization.

Benjamin Franklin’s life embodied the possibilities and contradictions of eighteenth-century America. A printer, writer, scientist, inventor, diplomat, and revolutionary, he helped shape both the institutions and the identity of the United States. His achievements grew not from wealth or extensive formal schooling but from curiosity, ambition, and a belief that knowledge should serve the public good.

Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706, into a large family supported by his father’s candle- and soap-making business. His formal education ended when he was about ten, but he remained an eager reader. At twelve, he became an apprentice to his older brother James, a printer. Working in the print shop taught him a trade and introduced him to public debate. While still a teenager, Franklin secretly contributed witty essays to his brother’s newspaper under the name Silence Dogood, adopting the voice of a fictional widow.

After conflicts with James, Franklin left Boston in 1723 and settled in Philadelphia. He eventually established a successful printing business and became the publisher of the *Pennsylvania Gazette*. In 1732, he began publishing *Poor Richard’s Almanack*, which mixed calendars, practical information, humor, and memorable sayings about thrift and hard work. These publications made him prosperous and helped establish his reputation as an insightful observer of human behavior.

Franklin’s ambition extended beyond personal success. In 1727, he organized the Junto, a discussion group whose members explored ideas for self-improvement and civic reform. He helped establish the Library Company of Philadelphia, a subscription library, and promoted volunteer firefighting, education, and medical care. He also helped found the academy that developed into the University of Pennsylvania. These projects reflected his conviction that ordinary people, working together, could improve their communities.

Science offered another outlet for Franklin’s practical curiosity. His investigations of electricity earned international recognition. His famous 1752 kite experiment helped demonstrate the electrical nature of lightning, and his development of the lightning rod provided a way to protect buildings from strikes. He also invented bifocal glasses and developed the Franklin stove. Rather than patenting his inventions, he believed that useful discoveries should benefit others freely.

Franklin’s personal life was more complicated than his public image of cheerful wisdom might suggest. He formed a common-law marriage with Deborah Read in 1730, and their household included his son William, whose mother’s identity remains uncertain. Benjamin and Deborah had two children together, Francis and Sarah; Francis died of smallpox at the age of four. Franklin’s long absences overseas placed strains on family life. The American Revolution later caused a lasting rupture between Franklin and William, who remained loyal to Britain.

For much of his political career, Franklin sought cooperation within the British Empire. He served in the Pennsylvania Assembly and worked as a colonial representative in London. Over time, however, disputes over taxation and British authority persuaded him that reconciliation was no longer possible. Returning to Philadelphia in 1775, he joined the Continental Congress. The following year, he served on the committee responsible for drafting the Declaration of Independence and signed the completed document.

Franklin’s diplomatic work in France proved especially important to American independence. His scientific fame, conversational skill, and carefully cultivated image of plain American simplicity helped him win influential supporters. He played a central role in securing the French alliance of 1778, which brought vital military and financial assistance to the American cause. He later helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris of 1783, in which Britain recognized United States independence.

In his final years, Franklin continued to participate in public affairs. He attended the Constitutional Convention in 1787, encouraging compromise despite his age and declining health. His moral outlook also changed over his lifetime. Earlier, he had enslaved people and printed advertisements connected to slavery. He later became president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society and, in 1790, petitioned Congress to act against slavery and the slave trade. This evolution does not erase his earlier participation, but it is an essential part of understanding his legacy.

Franklin died in Philadelphia on April 17, 1790, at the age of eighty-four. His life left an enduring mark on science, journalism, education, diplomacy, and government. He was neither flawless nor consistent in every conviction, yet he repeatedly demonstrated the power of learning and the possibility of change. His most lasting achievement may be the example he offered of curiosity turned outward: a restless search for knowledge joined to the practical work of improving society.

Benjamin Franklin, born on January 17, 1706, in Boston, Massachusetts, stands as one of the most remarkable figures in American history—a testament to what curiosity, discipline, and ambition could achieve in the eighteenth century. The fifteenth of seventeen children born to a candle and soap maker, Franklin's origins were humble, yet his intellect and drive propelled him to extraordinary heights across multiple fields.

Franklin's formal education ended at age ten, but this proved no barrier to his insatiable appetite for learning. Apprenticed to his brother James as a printer, young Benjamin devoured books and taught himself writing through careful study and imitation of great essayists. At seventeen, seeking independence from his brother's strict oversight, he ran away to Philadelphia, the city that would become his lifelong home and the stage for his greatest achievements.

In Philadelphia, Franklin built a successful printing business, eventually publishing the famous "Poor Richard's Almanack," filled with witty aphorisms that still resonate today: "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise." His business acumen allowed him to retire from active printing at age 42, freeing him to pursue his true passions: science, invention, and public service.

As a scientist, Franklin's contributions were revolutionary. His famous kite experiment demonstrated the electrical nature of lightning, leading to his invention of the lightning rod. He also invented bifocal glasses, the Franklin stove, and made significant discoveries about the Gulf Stream. His scientific reputation earned him international acclaim and membership in prestigious scientific societies across Europe.

Franklin's civic contributions to Philadelphia were equally impressive. He founded the city's first public library, organized its first fire department, helped establish the University of Pennsylvania, and created the American Philosophical Society. These institutions reflected his belief in community improvement through practical innovation and collective effort.

Perhaps most significantly, Franklin became a pivotal figure in American independence. He served as a diplomat, securing crucial French support during the Revolutionary War—support that proved decisive in America's victory over Britain. He was the only person to sign all four major documents establishing the United States: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution. His diplomatic skills, combined with his charm and wit, made him beloved in French society and effective in securing vital resources for the fledgling nation.

In his later years, Franklin continued serving his country, participating in the Constitutional Convention of 1787 despite failing health. He also became an advocate for the abolition of slavery, presiding over the Pennsylvania Abolition Society—a notable evolution given that he had owned slaves earlier in his life.

Franklin died on April 17, 1790, at age 84, having lived a life of extraordinary breadth. He was simultaneously a printer, author, scientist, inventor, diplomat, and statesman—embodying the Enlightenment ideal of the versatile, rational individual dedicated to both personal improvement and public good. His autobiography, left unfinished at his death, remains a classic of American literature, chronicling his journey from humble beginnings to international renown while offering timeless wisdom on self-improvement and civic virtue.

Franklin's legacy endures not merely in the institutions he founded or the inventions he created, but in the American ideal he embodied: that through hard work, curiosity, and dedication to the common good, an individual could rise to shape the course of history.

## Abstract

The presidency combines extensive decision-making, public communication, and continuous responsibility for national affairs. These features make presidential well-being an important subject for political science and leadership studies. This paper examines how the structure of presidential work shapes the demands placed on the person holding office and considers practices that support clear judgment and sustained performance. Drawing on research in executive leadership, occupational health, and political institutions, it argues that thoughtful scheduling, trusted counsel, physical activity, and periods for reflection can help presidents meet the office’s demands. ## Introduction

The president of the United States holds an office with broad responsibilities and a highly visible public role. A president may meet with advisers, review policy options, communicate with the public, and respond to developments in domestic and international affairs within the same day. This combination of duties makes the presidency a useful case for studying how people carry out demanding leadership roles over time [Source One].

Presidential well-being matters because executive decisions can shape public policy and national priorities. A president’s ability to listen, evaluate information, and communicate clearly supports the work of government. This paper examines the demands associated with presidential service and the practices that can sustain effective leadership. It argues that personal routines and institutional support work together: individual habits can aid sound judgment, while a well-organized executive branch can make presidential attention more effective.

## The Structure of Presidential Work

Presidential work is broad in scope. The president serves as head of state, chief executive, commander in chief, and a leading voice in national political life. Each role involves distinct forms of attention and communication. In one setting, a president may study technical information; in another, the president may speak to a national audience or confer with foreign leaders [Source Two].

The presidency also has a continuous character. Public affairs proceed across the calendar, while the president’s schedule includes both planned events and emerging matters. This pattern calls for sustained concentration and the ability to move between topics. Research on senior leadership suggests that work design, access to reliable information, and clear decision procedures can influence how leaders use their attention [Source Three].

Public visibility adds another dimension. Presidential words and actions receive close attention from citizens, journalists, public officials, and institutions. This visibility gives presidential communication particular reach. It also makes preparation, careful listening, and consistent public engagement valuable elements of the role [Source Four].

## Decision-Making and Well-Being

Sound decision-making depends on more than access to information. Leaders also benefit from time to consider options, hear informed perspectives, and clarify priorities. A structured process can support these tasks by identifying the question at hand, presenting relevant evidence, and making room for discussion among advisers [Source Five].

Well-being has a practical place in this process. Sleep, regular movement, nutritious meals, and moments for reflection can contribute to alertness and steady attention. These practices are relevant across occupations, and they hold particular value for people whose work involves frequent judgment and communication [Source Six]. Presidential schedules can make such routines a deliberate part of executive planning.

A president’s personal habits operate within an institutional setting. Advisers, agency leaders, and staff members help gather information and coordinate the work of government. Clear channels for consultation allow the president to hear perspectives from specialists and public officials. Delegation also enables members of the executive branch to carry out responsibilities assigned to their offices [Source Seven].

## Practices That Support Presidential Service

Several practices can support sustained presidential performance. First, a well-designed schedule can balance meetings, briefings, public appearances, and time for review. Protected periods for focused work allow a president to consider important questions without frequent transitions. Regular planning can also help staff coordinate the flow of information [Source Eight].

Second, a strong advisory process can improve the quality of executive deliberation. Advisers with varied expertise can explain the available evidence, outline possible courses of action, and identify relevant considerations. A president who invites careful discussion can draw on the knowledge of the wider executive team. Research on leadership groups emphasizes the value of clear roles and constructive exchange [Source Nine].

Third, personal routines can support the daily work of the office. Physical activity, consistent sleep schedules, and opportunities for quiet reflection may help maintain energy and focus. These practices do not determine policy outcomes; rather, they contribute to the conditions in which leaders carry out their duties [Source Ten].

Finally, institutional continuity matters. Established procedures for briefings, decision records, and communication can provide a dependable framework for presidential work. Such procedures help staff members coordinate their contributions and give the president a coherent view of issues requiring attention [Source Eleven].

## Institutional and Ethical Considerations

Discussion of presidential well-being should respect both personal privacy and public accountability. The public has a legitimate interest in the president’s capacity to fulfill the duties of the office. At the same time, personal health information deserves appropriate confidentiality. A balanced approach can focus on functional responsibilities, institutional support, and the quality of executive decision processes [Source Twelve].

The presidency also depends on cooperation across institutions. Congress, federal agencies, state governments, the courts, and the public each participate in the broader system of American governance. Presidential leadership therefore involves consultation and coordination as well as individual judgment. Recognizing this shared structure places executive well-being within a wider account of public service [Source Thirteen].

## Conclusion

The presidency calls for sustained attention, broad knowledge, and frequent communication. These features make presidential well-being relevant to the study of executive leadership and democratic governance. Thoughtful scheduling, informed counsel, healthy routines, and dependable institutional procedures can support a president’s capacity to serve.

Further study could compare presidential work patterns across administrations, examine the role of executive staff, or analyze how leaders organize time for reflection and consultation. Such research can deepen understanding of how the design of high-level public service supports capable leadership over time [Future Research Topic].

# Project Proposal: LearningBridge AI

## Project summary

**Duration:** 36 months  
**Initial scope:** 100 schools across two countries  
**Primary participants:** Students in grades 3 to 8 and their teachers  
**Estimated budget:** USD 2.4 million

LearningBridge AI will use machine learning and artificial intelligence to support better teaching and learning in underserved communities. The project will provide offline-capable learning tools and teacher support in local languages. It will work with education ministries and local communities to adapt the program to each setting.

AI will support teachers rather than replace them. Teachers will retain control over lessons and decisions about students.

## The need

Many schools face shortages of learning materials and trained teachers. Students may receive limited feedback or lessons that do not match their current skill levels. These challenges can be greater in rural areas and in communities where children learn in languages that are underrepresented in digital tools.

AI could help address some of these barriers. However technology alone cannot improve education. Tools must work with limited connectivity and local curricula. They must protect children’s data and support educators.

## Project goals

1. Improve student literacy and numeracy.
2. Help teachers identify learning needs and plan suitable lessons.
3. Expand access to learning resources in local languages.
4. Build local expertise in responsible education technology.
5. Generate reliable evidence about which approaches are effective.

## Main activities

### 1. Adaptive learning resources

Students will use tablets or shared school devices to access lessons and practice activities. A machine learning system will use student responses to recommend suitable next steps. Recommendations will be simple and visible to teachers.

The system will not make high-stakes decisions about students. Teachers will be able to review and change its suggestions.

### 2. Teacher support tool

Teachers will have access to an AI assistant that can help them:

- Create lesson plans aligned with the national curriculum.
- Adapt activities for different learning levels.
- Generate practice questions and reading materials.
- Translate or simplify selected content into local languages.
- Review class progress and identify students who may need support.

All generated content will be reviewed by teachers before classroom use. The project will provide training so teachers can assess accuracy and suitability.

### 3. Offline-first technology

The learning platform will be designed to function without a continuous internet connection. Schools will be able to download approved resources when connectivity is available and sync learning records later.

The project will use low-cost devices where possible. It will also explore options such as local school servers and printed materials for settings where device access is limited.

### 4. Local language and curriculum development

Local educators and language experts will help select and review learning materials. The project will prioritize languages and dialects chosen with participating communities. It will not assume that one language model or curriculum can serve every location.

### 5. Teacher development

Teachers and school leaders will receive practical training in:

- Using the learning platform.
- Interpreting student progress information.
- Reviewing AI-generated materials.
- Protecting student privacy.
- Maintaining meaningful human judgment in teaching.

## Implementation plan

### Phase 1: Co-design and preparation  
**Months 1 to 6**

- Select participating districts with education authorities.
- Consult teachers families students and local language experts.
- Review connectivity device access and existing curriculum.
- Establish data protection and safeguarding procedures.
- Develop and test initial learning materials.

### Phase 2: Pilot  
**Months 7 to 12**

- Introduce the tools in 20 schools.
- Train teachers and school leaders.
- Collect feedback on usability and local relevance.
- Fix technical and content problems before expansion.

### Phase 3: Expansion  
**Months 13 to 28**

- Expand to 100 schools.
- Provide ongoing teacher coaching.
- Monitor system performance and student access.
- Adapt the program based on school feedback.

### Phase 4: Evaluation and transition  
**Months 29 to 36**

- Measure learning and implementation outcomes.
- Share findings with ministries and communities.
- Prepare a plan for local ownership and future funding.
- Publish open resources where licensing and privacy rules allow.

## Evaluation

An independent evaluation will compare participating schools with similar schools that do not yet use the program. Where appropriate and approved by local partners the evaluation may use a phased rollout to ensure that comparison schools can receive the program later.

Measures will include:

- Student reading and mathematics results.
- Attendance and time spent on learning activities.
- Teacher confidence and lesson preparation time.
- Student access across gender disability language and location.
- Tool reliability and frequency of offline use.
- Student family and teacher satisfaction.

The project will establish baseline measures before rollout. It will set final targets with local education partners after the baseline is complete. Results will be reported honestly including negative or mixed findings.

## Ethics and safeguards

- Collect only the data required to deliver and evaluate the program.
- Obtain appropriate consent and explain data use in accessible language.
- Use encryption and role-based access controls.
- Set clear limits on data retention and deletion.
- Avoid facial recognition and other unnecessary surveillance.
- Test tools for unequal performance across language and student groups.
- Provide a way for students families and teachers to raise concerns.
- Require human review for consequential educational decisions.
- Do not sell student data or use it for advertising.

## Partnership and governance

The project will be governed by a steering group with representatives from education ministries local universities teacher organizations participating schools and community groups. A student and family advisory group will provide feedback throughout the project.

Local partners will lead curriculum decisions and guide the selection of languages. The project team will provide technical support and training. Responsibility for long-term operation will be agreed with education authorities before the end of the project.

By the end of the project participating schools will have practical tools for adapting learning activities and identifying student needs. Teachers will have greater access to curriculum-aligned resources and relevant training. Education authorities will have evidence to guide future decisions about responsible AI use.

The project will treat AI as one part of a broader effort to improve education. Its success will depend on strong teachers local leadership safe technology and sustained public investment.

# Project Proposal: Learning Together with AI

## 1. Project Summary

**Learning Together with AI** is an 18-month pilot designed to improve foundational literacy and numeracy in underserved schools in a developing country.

The project will support approximately 6000 students and 180 teachers across 30 schools. It will combine offline learning tools with machine learning that identifies learning gaps and recommends suitable practice activities.

The guiding principle is simple: **AI should strengthen teachers rather than replace them.**

The pilot will be developed with the education ministry and local communities. Expansion will depend on demonstrated learning gains and affordable operating costs.

## 2. The Challenge

Many schools face large classes and limited teaching materials. Teachers may struggle to identify each student’s needs or provide individual support.

Digital education projects can also fail when they depend on reliable internet access or content that does not match local languages and curricula.

This project addresses these constraints through shared devices and locally reviewed materials that work offline.

## 3. Objectives

The project will aim to:

- Improve foundational reading and mathematics skills.
- Help teachers identify learning gaps earlier.
- Reduce time spent preparing routine classroom materials.
- Improve access for students with disabilities and learners in remote communities.
- Establish whether AI-supported instruction offers better value than existing alternatives.

## 4. Proposed Solution

### Adaptive student practice

Students will use shared tablets during scheduled classroom rotations.

A lightweight machine learning model will estimate skill mastery from short assessments and practice responses. It will recommend activities from a curriculum-aligned content library.

Teachers will be able to review and override recommendations. Students will not be assigned permanent ability labels.

### Teacher planning assistant

An AI assistant will help teachers prepare lesson plans and differentiated exercises using approved curriculum materials.

Generated content will require teacher review before classroom use. The assistant will not make grading or disciplinary decisions.

### Learning progress dashboard

A simple dashboard will show which skills need additional instruction. It will recommend small-group activities without publicly ranking students.

Results will support teacher judgment rather than determine high-stakes outcomes.

### Local language and accessibility support

Local educators will adapt materials into selected languages and review them for accuracy and cultural relevance.

Accessible features will include adjustable text size and audio instructions. Speech-based tools will be introduced only where testing shows acceptable performance across local accents.

## 5. Implementation Plan

### Months 1–3: Co-design and preparation

- Select schools with local education authorities.
- Assess electricity and connectivity.
- Consult teachers and families.
- Conduct baseline learning assessments.
- Establish data protection rules and procurement requirements.

### Months 4–6: Development and testing

- Configure the offline platform.
- Adapt and review learning materials.
- Train teachers and school-based technical leads.
- Test usability and content safety in a small group of classrooms.

### Months 7–15: Classroom pilot

- Introduce regular supervised practice sessions.
- Provide ongoing teacher coaching.
- Maintain devices and monitor implementation.
- Correct inaccurate content and investigate unequal performance.

### Months 16–18: Evaluation and transition

- Conduct independent endline assessments.
- Compare results and costs with the control group.
- Share findings with participating communities.
- Develop an expansion plan only if evidence supports it.

## 6. Infrastructure and Sustainability

Each school will receive shared tablets and a local content server where needed. Solar charging will be provided where electricity is unreliable.

Core learning activities will work without continuous internet access. Updates and encrypted data transfers will occur when connectivity is available.

Open standards and exportable content will reduce vendor dependence. Local technicians will receive maintenance training. The education ministry will help assess long-term replacement and support costs.

The project will collect only data needed for learning support and evaluation.

Student records will use pseudonymous identifiers. Access will be restricted by role. Written agreements will prohibit advertising and unrelated model training using student data.

Children will not interact with unrestricted generative chatbots. All student-facing materials will come from a reviewed library.

The primary measure will be improvement on independent literacy and numeracy assessments. An illustrative target is an average gain of **0.15 standard deviations** above the comparison group. This is a target rather than a promised result.

Secondary measures will include:

- Student participation.
- Device uptime.
- Cost per student.
- Learning outcomes across demographic and language groups.
